meta.title: "He wouldn't say something silly": why a familiar face isn't proof | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to switch attention from the face to the content and ask "why is this true?" instead of believing just because someone famous said it. Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 10–16.

hero.headline: Does your child believe the face — or the facts?
hero.subheadline: "He's successful." "She's popular." "He wouldn't say something silly." A familiar face triggers trust before any content even appears — and your child believes because they recognise it, without ever checking the words.

media.alt: A child trusting a familiar face before they've even heard the content

pain.title: A face isn't proof
pain.body:
A familiar person can inspire trust — but that doesn't mean their words are right. They can be mistaken, know nothing about the topic, or simply be advertising something. The fact that we recognise a face says nothing about whether what it says is true.

This isn't being naive or gullible. The child is simply reacting to familiarity and status: a recognised face automatically feels like "one of us", someone to be believed. Without the skill of separating the two, they take in "who said it" instead of "what was said" — and trust shows up before any checking does.

The result — the child trusts the image, not the facts. They repeat, buy, and believe because "it's him/her" — not because there's anything true behind the words.

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 10–16 year olds. At this age, children are receptive to new thinking patterns and are still forming their views.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.
